name: Victor Zelinsky
languages: Polish (his father's; he understands more than he speaks)
equipment: Heavy coat: a brown canvas work coat with a blanket lining and a torn pocket
Crowbar: a three-foot pinch bar from the toolbox in the Ridgeview truck
Double-barrel shotgun: his father's old Stevens, which Ridgeview told him to bring for the watchman job
Tool kit: sockets, wrenches, a timing light, a feeler gauge
Work clothes or coveralls: green work pants, a Penn State sweatshirt from his sister
A rag that is never clean
A thermos of coffee and a lunch pail
A letter from Ridgeview Leisure Communities: 'Off-Season Watchman, Lantern Lake Estates, commencing Monday 19 September 1977, $3.10 per hour'
features: Up Before Dawn (Farm-Raised origin: he needs only 6 hours for a long rest and can't be surprised while awake in the last hour before sunrise; advantage on saves against exhaustion from hard work, cold and lost sleep; he notices without a check when animals are frightened, sick or behaving wrongly)

Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, when reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 instead; he ignores his first level of exhaustion and has advantage on CON saves against exhaustion, cold and hard labor)

Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something; he counts as one size larger for what he can carry, drag or lift, and can carry an unconscious adult at full speed)

Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, when he fails a fear check he gains no Dread, but on his next turn must move toward the source and attack it, or break what stands between them, or smash something nearby)
Trade: Longshoreman (Roughneck, 3rd level: advantage on Athletics checks to grapple, shove or hold a door, and a creature he grapples has disadvantage on checks to escape)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: he can find work at any garage and mechanics talk to him as one of their own; given a few minutes with a vehicle, generator or engine he can tell what is wrong with it, and whether someone made it that way)

personality.traits: I fix things. I say what I think, once, and then I shut up. I eat when there is food, because sometimes there isn't.
personality.ideals: A man who works should be able to live on it. Most of them can't, any more.
personality.bonds: My sister Halina in Nanticoke, who took me in when the shop closed. The farm in Wyoming County my father lost in 1958. My own two hands.
personality.flaws: I don't like rich men or their camps, and I came here ready to dislike everyone. I am going to be wrong about some of them, and slow to admit it.

appearance: Forty-four, thick through the shoulders and the middle, a broken-veined farm face, grey crew cut, hands like shovels with grease in every crack, a brown canvas work coat.
backstory: Victor Zelinsky grew up on a hill farm in Wyoming County, the son of a Polish miner who quit the anthracite to farm and lost the farm to the bank in 1958. Victor went into the mines himself at seventeen, came out after a roof fall in 1959, and has fixed engines ever since: a Wilkes-Barre Chevrolet dealer's service bay for sixteen years, until the dealership closed in May. Ridgeview Leisure Communities hired him through an ad in the Scranton paper as off-season watchman for Lantern Lake Estates, to start Monday, $3.10 an hour and a trailer by the gate when the trailer comes; Gene Marcotte brought him up on Friday to see the place. He thinks the camp is a rich man's toy and the development is worse, and he needs the job. He can tell what is wrong with any engine on the Neck by its sound. (Hook: work. He is the one who will know, at once, exactly what was done to the cars, and what it would take to undo it.)
